whyThisMatters: Real development decisions are fast — a PR, a dependency, a CI alert, and you don't always get time to research whether it's genuine. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a popular-looking package, a familiar reviewer handle, a routine-looking CI notification. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why reading a PR's diff carefully doesn't tell you what a new dependency does at install time.
Ask why a familiar-looking reviewer handle or a high download count doesn't prove a package or comment is safe.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is trusting anything wrapped in familiar developer workflow — a plausible download count, a familiar-looking handle, a routine notification style — without checking the actual publish history or domain. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.text: Opened GitHub Directly Instead Of Link
Ran Unknown Code In Isolated Environment
Clicked Re-Authorize Link In PR Comment
Ran Setup Script From Unsolicited Outreach
Re-Entered Git Token Via Email Link
Granted Admin Access To Unknown App
Assumed Popular Name Meant Safe Package

bubbles.note: Reading the diff carefully is good practice, but it doesn't reveal what a new dependency does at install time — still check the package's own history separately.
Running unknown code in an isolated environment is a strong safety net, but it's still safer to verify the source first rather than relying on isolation alone.
A familiar-looking handle can be a near-identical typosquat — the exact spelling matters more than how familiar the name feels.
A plausible download count is easy to fake or reach quickly with a freshly-popular-looking package — check the maintainer's actual history instead.

bubbles.text: Checked Official Marketplace For Extension Update
Rotated Secrets Via Vault UI, Not Email
Required Signed Process Before Emergency Deploy
Installed AI Extension From Link Outside Marketplace
Recognised Manager's Name On Deploy Request
bubbles.note: A familiar name on an urgent deploy request is exactly what this trick relies on — the domain, read in full, is still the real check.

bubbles.text: Fetched Runtime Secrets From The Vault, Not Source
Required A Signed Commit Before Merge
Validated Input On The Backend, Not Just The Frontend
Set A Rate Limit Before Shipping A New AI Endpoint
Hardcoded An API Key Into The Repository
Shipped An AI Feature With No Token Or Cost Limit
Used HTTPS For The Public-Facing API Only
bubbles.note: Encrypting external traffic is necessary but not sufficient — zero trust means TLS on internal service-to-service traffic too, not just what's internet-facing.
